title: Chapter 10: Her Own Crossing Log
content: Page sixty-three will not lie flat.

Wren has tried the brick. She has tried the sugar bowl and the second brick. The book is four hundred and two pages of green cloth and river-swollen paper, and the water it took on in 2019 has made every page in the middle curl toward the spine like something breathing.

She moves the lamp closer. She sets the phone face down across two dictionaries, lens at the corner of the page, and taps the screen with a knuckle. The shutter is a dry click. Then the page is in the phone and out of the weather.

Two in the morning. The kitchen table is a small factory. Banker's box on the floor with forty-one photocopied files inside, each one wearing a routing slip like a hat. Phone on the right. Between them, the log.

On Friday, Hollis Drane told her that a Form 9 without an underlying record was a bare assertion, and that a bare assertion could sit in his drawer until the river ran dry. He said it the way he says everything, gently, as if he were sorry for the drawer.
So she is building an underlying record. Four hundred and two pages of one.

At twelve pages an hour, with five minutes a page and no stopping, that is thirty-four hours. The phone has sixty-one gigabytes free and each photograph is four megabytes and the folder cannot go anywhere else. She has decided it will not go anywhere else. The cloud is a company, and a company is a place where things go to stop existing.
At 2:40 the phone buzzes against the dictionaries and she has to lift it off the page to read it.

Mars: are you doing the whole thing tonight.
Wren: no.
Mars: how many pages.
Wren: 402.
Mars: that is 50 hours. you did the math.
Wren: I did the math.
Mars: sleep is also a record. it is the record of a person still alive.
Wren puts the phone face down again and stops answering.
The book has rules. Her grandfather wrote them on the inside of the front board in 1975, in the same small hand he used for everything after that.
Never cross out a name. If you cannot spell it, ask. Pencil only for the margin. The book does not go in the water.
She used to think that last one was a joke about the ferry. Now she reads it and hears a man telling himself something for fifty-one years.

The tin smells like rope and old paper and the inside of a tackle box. The ribbon is red and frayed where he used it to mark the day, and the day is still marked. 11 September, the Friday. The last ordinary page in the book.
The columns are ruled in ink gone brown. DATE. SOULS. WEATHER. WATER. FARE.

His hand is small and leans left. In 1975 it leaned right. She finds the first page in his hand, 3 May 1975, a crossing at six in the morning, weather clear, fare fifteen cents, and the loops in the word clear are young and showing off.
By 1988 it is a ballpoint. By 1994 it is the same pen he kept by the door until last month, the one with the chip out of the barrel where he used to bite it.
She photographs in order from the back, because the back is where her names are.
The last entry is 12 September 2026. Nine souls. 9:40 p.m. Weather, clear. The water column is blank.

He never filled it in. He wrote nine names and left the water empty, because at 9:47 the river came up faster than a man could write, and the last thing he did with the book was put it back in the tin.
Wren looks at the blank for a long time. The lamp hums. Somewhere out on the river a piece of the cable housing ticks against the frame, the way it has ticked every night since somebody cut it.
Then she takes a pencil from the jelly jar and writes, small, in the water column: +6. 9:47.
She does not sign it. There is no column for who wrote what.

The fares are the part she did not expect. Five cents until 1979. Ten cents until 1991. A quarter after that, and a quarter for thirty-five years, because her grandfather did not believe in charging more for the same water.

Beside the quarters, in a hand that shrinks a little every year, the word IOU. Four hundred and eleven of them. Half of Mill Street crossed on credit, and he never wrote a name next to a single debt, as if the debt belonged to the town and not to any one person in it.
She photographs those too. She does not know why. It seems like the kind of thing that ought to exist twice.
At three she starts matching names.

The files from Mars are in order, oldest first. Owen Pike, 1994, taken off the bank at Mile 9. She finds him on 14 May at 6:12 a.m., one soul, weather clear, water +2, fare a quarter. Eight minutes later the gate opened for silt. In the margin, in pencil, two words.
no siren

She turns the page. She goes back to the start of 1975 and reads every margin forward, and the words are there nineteen times. Nineteen afternoons and evenings when the water came up and nothing announced it. Nineteen times her grandfather wrote the same two words in pencil, as if a pencil were a thing that could be taken back.
The last of them is 2 August 2019, the night the river came into the boat shed and took the paint off the hull and did not take the boat.

She saw one of those marks when she was nine and asked him what it meant. He said the river came up. She asked why it was in pencil. He said because a pen would make it official, and it was not official, and that was the whole problem, and then he turned the page.

By half past five she has matched thirty-one of the forty-one. Anna Voss Rusk crossed in 2003 as Anna K. Voss, nine years old, fare paid by her mother. Harlan Deeds crossed on his birthday in 1997 and the next column says, in her grandfather's hand, sang. Deacon Ross crossed four hundred and six times. He is in the book more than he is in his own file.

Ten files have no page. She writes their names on the back of an envelope and underlines the word none. Some of them went in above the ferry, at Mile 11, where the river bends and the book cannot see. The book is only what crosses. Everything else is the county's problem, and the county has a drawer for that.

One of the ten is a woman who crossed on her wedding day in 1979 under a name she kept for eleven months. The file has the second name. The book has the first. Wren finds her by the date, because names change and dates are stubborn, and she circles the entry, and then she puts the pencil down without writing anything in the margin, because a note there would be a correction and the rule says never.

At twenty to six she stops to charge the phone and stands in the doorway with a cup of coffee, and the town is a row of dark windows and one lit one, Ruthie's, where the light is on and the door has been unlocked since half past five and the ledger is already open on the counter. Wren thinks about walking over. She thinks about how a person in a diner at that hour is a person with a story about why, and she does not want to be that yet.
At six her eyes start sliding off the lines, so she stands up and eats a piece of bread over the sink and looks at the east bank getting grey.
Then she goes back to 2002, because she knows what is there.
26 March. No souls. Weather, ice. Fare, none. In the weather column, in pencil, because he broke his own rule: girl born 4:20 a.m.
He wrote the time before he wrote her name. He wrote her name on the next line, in ink, Wren Aubrey, and then he closed the book and did not open it again for three days.

2011 is harder. She finds the week in October and there are crossings on every page, because a ferry does not stop for a funeral. On the Thursday the weather column says rain, and in the margin, in pencil, the only time in fifty-one years that he wrote anything about himself.
long day

Wren puts the pencil down. She sits with her hands flat on the table until the shaking stops, and then she picks the pencil back up, because the front of the book is still there and she has not seen it yet.
She saves the front for last, the way you save the last of something.
The front board is cracked at the hinge. The bookplate inside is a rectangle of glue and foxed paper. It says: AUBREY FERRY, MILE NINE, SABLE RIVER. BEGUN APRIL 1908.
The first entry is 12 April 1908. Nine souls. Weather, rain. Water, high. Fare, free, first day.
Nine names in brown ink, in a hand that is not her grandfather's, and older than anything else in the house.
At the bottom of the page, in the same ink, a signature.
Maud Aubrey, ferryman.
Under it, in smaller letters, pressed hard enough to emboss the page beneath:
If I am lost, the book stays with the boat.
Wren sits back. The chair complains.

Nobody in her family has ever said the name Maud. Not at a funeral, not at Christmas, not in the stories her grandfather told about the flood of 1993, when he was forty-five and the water came up to the second step of the porch and he carried the book on his head across the yard.
A woman ran this ferry in 1908. A woman wrote the rule. And the rule has been kept for a hundred and eighteen years by men who never said her name out loud.
The county's first ferry license is dated 1911 and lists an operator as M. Aubrey, no first name spelled out, which is how a woman becomes an initial in a ledger and then a gap in a family.

Wren reads the line again. Then she carries the book down to the landing in the dark, because that is where the rule says it lives, and she puts it back in the biscuit tin under the counter and puts the rubber band around it twice.
The ferry is black against a grey river. The cable hangs low and drips. Past the bend the gate is quiet, holding back a lake the town is not allowed to see.

She walks back up the bank. The house is colder than it was. His chair is where it was. The television is where it was. She has not moved anything, and she has begun to suspect that moving anything would be a kind of filing.
In the kitchen she opens the phone, deletes the folder she made at midnight, and makes a new one.
Then she photographs page two.
highlight: Wren starts photographing the crossing log, four hundred and two pages of her grandfather's hand.
